title: Astros’ Carlos Correa to undergo season-ending ankle surgery
content:
HOUSTON — At 10:32 a.m. on Wednesday, Carlos Correa crutched his way into a crestfallen Houston Astros clubhouse. A boot covered his left ankle. A chair awaited him against the wall, where Correa sometimes delivers a state of the team address. Correa rested his crutches there, decided to stand and described how his season had come to an abrupt end.

“Hitting in the cage, normal day, feeling great, went through my whole routine,” Correa said. “Took a swing and just felt a pop. It completely snapped on me. Fell to the ground and couldn’t put any weight on it.

“I felt a loud pop. I heard it and felt it. Right away, I knew something was wrong.”

Correa tore a tendon in his left ankle while taking batting practice before Tuesday’s 2-1 win against the Los Angeles Dodgers. He will undergo season-ending surgery within the next week, dealing a crippling blow to an Astros club already decimated by injuries.

“It’s really hard,” manager Joe Espada said. “Talking to Carlos this morning was just really, really hard for what he means to this team, this organization, personally to me as his manager, as a friend. It sucks.”

Correa did not specify which tendon is torn, nor did he have a date for his surgery. Correa said he will seek a few other opinions, but described the tendon as “completely torn.” Recovery time, according to Correa, is six to eight months.

“It’s a gut punch,” said general manager Dana Brown.

“The team is still built to win. No doubt about it, you’re losing your captain on the field, and you’re losing the production that he’s bringing. But he’ll still be around. We’ll still have his support. But we still have a really good team and feel like it’s still built to win.”

On Wednesday, Correa became the 15th Astros player to reach the injured list, joining a group that includes ace Hunter Brown, closer Josh Hader, shortstop Jeremy Peña, center fielder Jake Meyers and catcher Yainer Diaz. Correa, Brown, Diaz and Meyers were all in Houston’s Opening Day lineup.

Correa had been one of the few constants amid that chaos. Before Tuesday’s injury, Correa played in 32 of the Astros’ first 35 games. His .787 OPS trailed only slugger Yordan Alvarez and resurgent first baseman Christian Walker for the team lead. Correa’s defense at shortstop and third base has remained elite.

Two early-season injuries to Peña had forced Correa to play more shortstop and, more recently, become the lineup’s leadoff hitter. Peña, who strained his hamstring last month, is nearing a minor-league rehab assignment and could return to the major-league roster late next week.

When he does, Houston can start to fill Correa’s massive void. Peña will reprise his role as the everyday shortstop, while Isaac Paredes will take Correa’s place at third base. The Astros attempted to trade Paredes this winter, but could not find a return package they felt justified moving a valuable depth piece.

Now, holding on to Paredes may prove to be a season-saving decision.

“Thank God we have the depth still in the infield,” Brown said.

That alone will aid in absorbing Correa’s impact on the field.

Correa’s injury is the latest in a career full of them. Plantar fasciitis in both feet caused him to miss time in 2023 and 2024 while with the Minnesota Twins. Back issues plagued him early in his career with Houston, as did a broken rib in 2019.

After the 2021 season, concerns about Correa’s surgically-repaired right ankle caused both the San Francisco Giants and New York Mets to void $300 million free-agent agreements with him.

When the Astros re-acquired Correa from the Twins last August, he moved to third base — in part — to reduce the wear and tear on his lower half. His arrival back in Houston, as an unquestioned clubhouse leader, helped Correa “fall in love with baseball more than ever.”

Now, it is taken away from him.
